 Weekend Box Office: Godzilla Minus Zero Roars to Monster Opening
 Takashi Yamazaki's hotly anticipated kaiju sequel led the way as six new films made the top 10.
 By
 Erik Childress 
 | Published November 8, 2026 
 TAGGED AS: Box Office , movies , news 
 When you go over the box office list this week, the story may not be The Cat in the Hat failing to make much of a dent with audiences. Look a little closer and you will see not one, but two non-English films in the top 10; one of them ruling them all and on its way to becoming one of the all-timers. Plus a non-music documentary setting a path to a milestone. What a week!
 King of the Crop: Godzilla Minus Zero Roars to a Monster Opening 
 There have been many successful American versions of Godzilla over the years from Gareth Edwards’ reboot in 2014 to the Godzilla vs (or x ) Kong films. Even Roland Emmerich’s Godzilla was financially a success back in 1998. But arguably the best Godzilla film of all-time was released in 2023. Godzilla Minus One was at least the best since the 1954 original, critically speaking, and it had the third-best opening weekend ever at the time for a non-English-language feature. ( Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – Infinity Castle knocked it back to fourth.) Its sequel, Godzilla Minus Zero , just said “move aside even further” with a $31.6 million start, which is also the best start ever for GKids.
 That is the second-best non-English live-action opening ever, or the best for a live-action non-English film in any language other than Aramaic. It won’t take long for it to become the third-highest-grossing (again, live-action) film in that category ever, passing Life is Beautiful ($57.2 million). Godzilla Minus One finished less than $103,000 behind the Roberto Benigni film domestically. The Passion of the Christ and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon are the only live-action ones to ever surpass $100 million. ( Infinity Castle made over $135 million after a $70.6 million start.) Worldwide the reported $13-15 million production has made $63 million. So go Godzilla!
 Tales of the Top 10: The Cat in the Hat Disappoints, You Can See Everything Continues to Impress 
 The Theodor Geisel brand has proven to be very successful in the movies. You may know him better as Dr. Seuss, and the run began with the live-action version of How the Grinch Stole Christmas with Jim Carrey in 2000 grossing over $260 million domestic. The live-action The Cat in the Hat with Mike Myers followed in 2003 with a 10% critics score and just over $101 million domestic. It has been the only unsuccessful film in the Seuss run and a film deemed so bad that Geisel’s widow stopped any future live-action adaptation of Theodor’s work, including a once-planned sequel. From then on, Seuss went exclusively animated with Horton Hears a Who!, The Lorax , and 2017’s The Grinch , which grossed a collective $1.157 billion worldwide.
 So why not try to correct the past with an animated version of The Cat in the Hat with another SNL alum, Bill Hader, behind the voice and have it kick off the holiday movie season? Should be a solid cash cow for Warner Bros., right? Apparently not, as the film opened to a measly $20.5 million on the domestic side and another $10 million overseas — much lower than just the domestic openings of The Lorax ($70.2 million), The Grinch ($67.5 million), Horton ($45.0 million), and even the Myers version ($38.3 million). That’s not a great number for the $86 million production, which is going to need to put in some overtime to even approach ending Warner Bros. string of 13 straight films to not reach $100 million. No animated film released before December opening between $5-25 million has finished with five times its opening since The Polar Express turned $23.3 million into $162.7 million (against The Incredibles , no less) back in 2004. It’s looking like 14 in a row for Warner Bros., who may be looking forward to Dune: Part Three even more than the fans are.
 Angel Studios offered a promise this past week saying that their films going forward will have no sex, no nudity, no profanity of any kind for films aimed at kids under 12, and no F-bombs for discerning adults, either. It also won’t take the name of God in vain. This weekend they released the Revolutionary War “action-musical from four-time Grammy-winning music group For King and Country.” That war where over 25,000 Americans died (but may not have had sex or sworn) may just be their new bread-and-butter, as Drummer Boy opened to $9.3 million, making it their third-best live-action opening after Sound of Freedom ($19.6 million) and this year’s Young Washington ($19.3 million).
 The No. 1 film in the country last week fell back to fourth place this weekend. The fact that it was ever No. 1 is still one of the many accomplishments of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything . Here’s another for you: It lost 770 theaters this weekend and still fell only 23% to $8.8 million. Its 24-day total is now $79.8 million, passing March of the Penguins ’ domestic gross of $77.4 million and making it the second-highest-grossing non-music-based doc of all time. Last week we showed how the only October releases after 17 days between $60-70 million to have a $10+ million third weekend and hit $100 million were Argo, The Ring , and Captain Phillips . Looking at the latter film on that list, it had $82.4 million after an $8.4 million fourth weekend. The Social Network , which came up just shy with $96.9 million, had $72.9 million after 24 days and a $7.2 million fourth. In other words, You Can See Everything is currently on pace to cross $100 million at the domestic box office. 
 Sony’s release of Ramayana: Rise of a Legend rebounded from some early negative critic reviews, jumping from 44% to 77%. Reportedly the most expensive Indian film ever made, it had an $8.6 million weekend, which just cracked the top 10 of the highest non-English openings of all time, knocking out Instructions Not Included ($7.8 million). That’s two non-English films in the top 10 this week. With pre-shows on Wednesday, the film is up to $12.1 million. Dhurandhar: The Revenge opened to $10.03 million in March and finished with $28.1 million. Globally, Ramayana has made over $55 million. Sony’s release of Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil is now over $409 million worldwide and about to move into eighth place on the all-time horror list.
 The math on Clayface is looking OK for Warner Bros. and DC, especially after a pretty respectable third weekend drop of just 39.3%. That amounted to $6.68 million and gives it $56.6 million in 17 days. Superman made $56.1 million on its first day, but whatever. Clayface has much more in common with Jackass: The Movie , which was up to $53.1 million after 17 days in October 2002. The film about guys who also had their bodies mutilated was there after a $7.1 million third weekend. If it continues along that pace, Clayface could get over $70 million and possibly even surpass Supergirl’ s $72.3 million domestic finish. Thankfully Clayface cost much less (as low as $30 million or as high as $44 million) and it just crossed $109 million worldwide. So on both the low and high end of the budget, the film is in profit. Financially, it’s not a disaster by any stretch in itself, but it may also be the second film in a row of the Gunnverse to globally gross less than $150 million.
 Even with the animated challenge from Warner Bros. and Dr. Seuss, Laika Studios’ Wildwood lost only 22% of its business from last week. Another $6.8 million this weekend brings its 17-day total to $39.8 million. That puts it between other October family releases The Book of Life ($8.2 million third weekend, $40.4 million in 17 days) and Goosebumps 2: Haunted Halloween ($7.2 million, $38.1 million). Those films had big drop-offs in their fourth weeks, but even with a PG-13 Ebenezer coming next week, the PG-13 Wildwood released by Fathom Entertainment could be on track to best both of their final grosses and finish between $50-60 million. It could possibly even mount a challenge to Paranorman ’s $56 million and become Laika’s second-highest-grossing domestic release after Coraline . Fathom also released the biopic Jimmy this weekend, with KJ Apa as Mr. Stewart. It opened to $2.2 million and may have just cracked the top 10, but stay tuned for final estimates Monday.
 Wild Horse Nine is the second time one of Martin McDonough’s films have opened wide rather than get platformed. The previous time was Seven Psychopaths by CBS Films (his follow-up to In Bruges ), which opened in 1,480 theaters to $4.17 million. This is McDonough’s third go with Searchlight Pictures, who started his last film, The Banshees of Inisherin , in four theaters (the fourth-best per-theater average of 2022 with $46,114) and ultimately saw it gross over $10.5 million. They also released his Oscar-winning Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri in 2017 (the fifth-best PTA of 2017 with $80,542) and saw it gross over $54.5 million. Wild Horse Nine opened in 1,100 theaters to $6 million. Next week the expected awards contender expands to over 2,000 theaters, which could keep it in the top 10 for another week. It made another $6.6 million overseas.
 Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson’s Wicker may end up being just the third-highest-grossing Sundance premiere of the year, but that is a solid place to be after Buddy and The Invite both grossed over $26 million. After $3.2 million this weekend, Wicker is at $19.7 million, making it the fourth-highest-grossing Sundance premiere since the pandemic. We’ll see if this success continues next year as the fest has its first year in Boulder, Colorado.
 Beyond the Top 10: Street Fighter Gets Nudged Out 
 Paramount’s Street Fighter may have gotten barely knocked out of the top 10 with $2.15 million. That brings its 24-day total to $57.4 million, ranking it among the worst opening-to-total multiples of the year (1.865 to date) for films in over 3,000 theaters. It’s down there with The Bride! (1.807), Scream 7 (1.916), The Dog Stars (1.940), Supergirl (1.950) and Scary Movie (1.992). Rob Savage’s Other Mommy got over the double multiple hump and continues to be in the million-dollar club in its fifth weekend, making $1.55 million to bring its total to $58.3 million.
 Along with the success of You Can See Everything , A24 just had some more with a nice launch for Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid . The film currently boats a perfect, Certified Fresh 100% on the Tomatometer and opened to $390,000 in six theaters. That amounts to the fifth-best per-theater average of 2026 ($65,000) behind The Moment ($106,985), The History of Concrete ($90,892), Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($80,252), and Netflix’s La bola negra ($69,405), which moved into 473 theaters this weekend and made $975,000, bringing its total to $2.4 million. Club Kid expands further next weekend and goes nationwide Thanksgiving week.
 Just missing the per-theater average top 10 this year was Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky . Amazon/MGM went the platform route into just seven theaters this weekend, where it grossed $345,000 for a $49,283 PTA. It expands further over the next two weeks and could end up being one of this holiday season’s sleepers as well as an awards contender. IFC’s release of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson’s follow-up to Ghostlight , Mouse , played in three theaters and grossed $42,000 for a $14,000 PTA.
 On The Vine: Ebenezer , How to Rob a Bank , and Lots More 
 Johnny Depp returns to theaters courtesy of director Ti West for his new adaptation of A Christmas Carol , Ebenezer , from Paramount. David Leitch, the director of Deadpool 2 and Bullet Train , has Nicholas Hoult and his gang of merry robbers in How to Rob a Bank from Amazon/MGM. Jim Caviezel goes to war for ranchers in Ghost Soldier from Sony, and Maika Monroe may be a Victorian Psycho for Bleecker Street. Neon has Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller in James Gray’s acclaimed Paper Tiger (86%). Finally, Pedro Almodovar’s Bitter Christmas (87%) from Sony Classics rounds it out.
